name: Drought / water-deficit stress
summary: Water deficit is a measured exposure-response diagnosis, not a synonym for drooping leaves. Cannabis studies document leaf-angle change, chlorosis, reduced expansion, cultivar-specific wilting or shedding, and growth or yield effects, but the label requires plant-linked root-zone moisture and irrigation history plus exclusion of salinity, hypoxia, heat/VPD, root restriction, vascular injury, and root disease.
indicators: Substrate or soil moisture is measurably below the established irrigation target while the plant shows water-deficit stress
Canopy wilt or reduced expansion coincides with a documented dry root zone and improves after appropriate rehydration
Leaf area or biomass growth declines during a sustained measured water deficit without root rot evidence
A time-linked root-zone measurement shows water content below that plant and production system's established irrigated baseline while leaf posture or growth changes develop.

Repeated side-view images show fan-leaf blades and petioles moving downward relative to their own turgid baseline and a matched irrigated control; absolute leaf angle from one frame is not diagnostic.
The temporal pattern begins after a documented missed, blocked, insufficient, or intentionally withheld irrigation event and is strongest in the zone supplied by that event or emitter.

In one controlled flowering experiment, visible wilt followed sustained drying and was accompanied by veinal chlorosis that began on older leaves and occurred less strongly on newer leaves across the plant; this is study-specific, not a universal color signature.
Sustained measured deficit can reduce leaf area, shoot expansion, total biomass, or seed/flower yield even when acute wilt is weak or delayed.
Cultivars can differ in stomatal closure, midday relative water content, wilting score, leaf retention, and recovery, so matched-plant context carries more weight than a generic droop class.

After careful rehydration, water status and posture may improve while photosynthesis or growth remains depressed; different recovery rates support a temporal water-response link but do not exclude coexisting injury.
exclusions: Do not label drought from one wilted, chlorotic, curled, or drooping image without a plant-linked moisture measurement and irrigation timeline.
If the root zone is adequately moist at representative center, edge, and depth locations while wilt persists, investigate other causes rather than assuming hidden drought.
Measure root-zone EC and source-water/fertilizer history because elevated salts can create osmotic stress even when volumetric water content appears adequate.
Exclude overwatering or hypoxia using moisture history, drainage, aeration, odor, and root color and firmness; drought and hypoxia can produce overlapping canopy wilt.

Inspect roots and crown for brown, slimy, sloughed, necrotic, sunken, or internally discolored tissue and obtain laboratory confirmation when Pythium, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, or vascular disease remains plausible.

Record air temperature, leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow because high atmospheric demand or heat/light injury can change midday leaf posture without a primary soil-water deficit.

Inspect intact root-ball geometry and irrigation wetting because root binding, hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, blocked emitters, and small root volume can create localized water shortage with distinct corrective needs.
Exclude broken stems, girdling, transplant damage, pest injury, and normal cultivar or circadian leaf posture using crown inspection, organism scouting, matched controls, and time-of-day replication.

progression.description: Measured root-zone water content declines; stomatal regulation and transpiration can change before a reliable visible symptom appears.
Leaf angle or turgor changes relative to the same plant's baseline and matched controls, often varying with time of day, VPD, cultivar, and acclimation.
Photosynthesis, expansion, leaf area, or leaf retention may decline; chlorosis was observed in one controlled flowering protocol but is not specific.
Prolonged or stronger deficit can reduce biomass or yield, with magnitude depending on genotype, stage, environment, root volume, and protocol.
Water status and visible posture may recover sooner than photosynthesis or growth; incomplete or absent recovery triggers root, crown, EC, and vascular investigation.

lookAlikes: Normal cultivar-specific or circadian leaf posture
Hydrophobic substrate, preferential flow, or blocked emitter
Transplant shock or mechanical root loss
Potassium or nitrogen deficiency with marginal/older-leaf symptoms
Camera angle, lens perspective, or time-of-day mismatch
confirmation: Assign a plant identifier and capture the whole canopy from fixed front and side positions plus representative fan leaves, substrate surface, container, emitter, drainage, and root-zone context with a metric scale and neutral color reference.

Measure volumetric water content or a validated medium-appropriate moisture proxy at multiple center, perimeter, and depth positions; log calibrated method, timestamp, last irrigation, applied volume, runoff, and the crop-specific baseline.

Repeat leaf-angle or posture images at the same time of day and camera geometry before deficit, during the suspected event, immediately before rehydration, and after rehydration; compare a matched same-cultivar irrigated plant.
Record air and leaf temperature, relative humidity, VPD, PPFD, and airflow at each capture so atmospheric demand can be separated from root-zone water availability.
Measure root-zone EC and pH, inspect emitter output and wetting uniformity, and document intact root-ball volume and boundary condition before disturbing roots.

Inspect roots, crown, and stem cross-sections for decay, lesions, odor, sloughing, galls, insects, girdling, and internal discoloration; send plant-linked samples for pathogen or nematode testing when indicated.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, single-timepoint, unmatched, sensor-unlinked, generated, vendor, anecdotal, unverified, and rights-unclear captures out of the confirmed class and every automated training split.
immediateActions: Verify root-zone moisture, emitter function, wetting uniformity, EC, and drainage before applying water solely because the canopy appears wilted.

Preserve pre-correction images and measurements, then rehydrate conservatively according to medium and root condition while monitoring runoff and avoiding abrupt saturation of a compromised root zone.
Segregate or flag plants with root/crown decay, vascular discoloration, galls, or insects for diagnostic review rather than treating them as simple drought.
correctivePlan: Correct the documented delivery failure, insufficient volume/frequency, hydrophobicity, root-volume mismatch, or excessive atmospheric demand using production-system-specific measurements rather than a universal schedule.

Trend moisture, leaf posture, water status where available, EC, new growth, and root health after correction; persistent decline requires reassessment for salinity, hypoxia, structural injury, and disease.
Do not intentionally reproduce a published drought endpoint as a corrective or production recipe; controlled experimental stress thresholds are not validated as universal safe practices.
prevention: Build cultivar-, stage-, container-, substrate-, and environment-specific irrigation baselines from calibrated measurements and plant-linked observations.
Audit emitter output, pressure, wetting footprint, drainage, root volume, substrate rewetting behavior, and sensor placement before high-demand periods.
Use fixed-view, fixed-time healthy reference captures so normal circadian and cultivar posture can be distinguished from a developing water deficit.
warnings: Do not use one wilted photograph as proof of drought; retain it only as an unconfirmed visual lead until plant-linked water evidence and exclusions are available.
Wilting, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, slow growth, and rehydration response are supportive but not specific; drought remains an exposure-linked diagnosis.

The approximately 11-day drying period, -1.5 MPa plant-water-potential endpoint, and roughly 52% leaf-angle change came from one controlled flowering chemovar and must not be used as universal thresholds.

Hemp cultivars differ substantially in soil-drying and VPD responses, and observation time changes apparent wilting; a model must not learn one canopy posture as genotype-independent drought ground truth.
Published effects on cannabinoid concentration, biomass, and yield vary by genotype, severity, stage, and protocol; this diagnostic profile does not recommend intentional drought stress.

No licensed, plant-linked Cannabis drought progression image or verified diagnostic video with reusable item-level rights was located for this batch; publisher figures remain citations only and media stays empty.

sources.title: Genotypic Variation in Photosynthesis and Biomass Partitioning Underlies Agronomic Performance and Cannabinoid Profile in Cannabis sativa Under Drought
supportedClaims: Water deficit imposed at early flowering reduced leaf area and affected plant water status, photosynthesis, biomass partitioning, and cannabinoid response in a genotype-dependent way.
Different Cannabis genotypes used different physiological drought responses, so visual canopy appearance or one moisture reading is not a universal drought-severity scale.

sources.title: Variation in Hydric Response of Two Industrial Hemp Varieties (Cannabis sativa) to Induced Water Stress
supportedClaims: Two hemp varieties showed notably different water-stress strategies, including partial stomatal closure in one and rapid leaf shedding in another.
The genotype-dependent responses support using substrate moisture and plant water-status context rather than a single visual symptom to identify water deficit.

sources.title: Increasing Inflorescence Dry Weight and Cannabinoid Content in Medical Cannabis Using Controlled Drought Stress
supportedClaims: In one controlled container-grown drug-type Cannabis experiment, fertigation was withheld during flowering week 7 until midday plant water potential reached approximately -1.5 MPa after 11 days; substrate volumetric moisture, plant water potential, photosynthesis, and leaf angle were measured against irrigated controls.

At the treatment endpoint, plants were visibly wilted and the measured indicator-leaf angle was approximately 52% greater than its initial angle; veinal chlorosis had appeared after about nine days, first on older leaves and to a lesser extent on newly formed leaves across the plant.

The day after re-fertigation, mean midday plant water potential recovered to the control level while net photosynthesis had only partially recovered, showing that response variables and recovery timing need not move together.

The timing, -1.5 MPa endpoint, leaf-angle change, chlorosis, and cannabinoid results come from one chemovar and one controlled flowering protocol; none is a universal Cannabis drought threshold, visual signature, or production recommendation.
The article figures are publisher-hosted copyrighted scientific content without a verified item-level reusable asset license, so they are citation evidence only and are not indexed as dataset media.

sources.title: Physiological screening for drought-tolerance traits among hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) cultivars in controlled environments and in field
sources.organization: Journal of Crop Improvement (Sheldon et al.)
supportedClaims: Progressive soil-drying trials found substantial cultivar differences in the fraction-of-transpirable-soil-water point at which hemp transpiration declined; five of thirteen cultivars closed stomata comparatively early.
A separate high-VPD screen found cultivar-specific limited-transpiration responses, with fitted VPD breakpoints ranging from 1.2 to 2.6 kPa among four responsive cultivars.

In a rainfed field comparison of six cultivars, wilting scores and relative water content differed among cultivars; Ha3ze, Carolina, and topped T1 had the lowest wilting scores during the reported midday observation period.
Wilting posture therefore depends on genotype, soil drying, atmospheric demand, observation time, and acclimation; the study does not establish one image-only drought threshold for Cannabis.
The publisher PDF and its plots do not provide verified reusable item-level media rights for this dataset, so no figure or frame is indexed as training or display media.

sources.title: Physiological and morphological responses of industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) to water deficit
sources.organization: Industrial Crops and Products (Gill et al.)
supportedClaims: An 85-day greenhouse experiment on industrial hemp cultivar Black Label compared moderate and extreme water deficit with a control and measured morphological, physiological, and biochemical responses.

Water deficit reduced total biomass and total seed yield, reduced stomatal opening and transpiration, increased water-use efficiency and proline accumulation, and still allowed plants to survive and produce filled seed under the tested conditions.

These single-cultivar endpoint responses support drought as a growth and yield stress but do not validate a universal visible severity scale, mortality expectation, or cannabinoid-production response for other Cannabis genotypes and stages.
The article is marked in copyright by its institutional repository; no image, figure, or video is indexed or copied as reusable media.
